## TL;DR

Review round 1 passed the engineering work but noted its captured screenshot showed the dashboard rather than the new-task needs-input message. I added a client-only shot fixture that seeds the same informational toast returned by the creation flow, declared a capture targeting that toast, and verified the rendered result with headless Playwright. The reviewer’s merge-tree note says the only conflict is the task’s own work file and that close-out resolves it from main, so it needs no code change. The fixture test and UI build pass; the final scoped check will bind this draft to the checked tree.

## Work and rationale

The original defect fix remains unchanged: CLI task body edits now run the shared asynchronous spec and human-step assessment after `body`, `section`, or `assignedTo` updates, matching the UI PATCH route. The command reports needs-input detail and lets the shared helper clear its own stale underspecified reason after the body is repaired. The new-task drawer surfaces the reason returned by the create endpoint in an informational toast. A focused CLI regression covers both raising and clearing that reason.

The review’s evidence concern was valid. My first browser pass confirmed the drawer could open but did not visibly show the changed toast; the task remained in a read-only preview, so I could not safely create a disposable task there. I avoided changing the product flow to make preview writes possible. Instead, I added a named preview fixture, `toast:taskNeedsInput`, to the normal shot-state registry and its application switch. It clears any existing toast state, inserts a representative informational message with missing sections, and stamps the fixture as applied. The fixture only changes client state in preview capture; it does not write a task or call the create API.

I declared a shot on the Work route with a highlight on `[role="status"]`, which is the toast’s accessible status surface. That makes the review capture point at the exact information introduced by the change. The toast text mirrors a real underspecified-body result: it names the missing Problem, Acceptance criteria, and Notes for AI sections. This is a representative UI state rather than a claim that the browser submitted a task.

## Approaches tried

I first confirmed the round-1 report and current task status using RepoOS and inspected the shot fixture registry and toast component. I added a fixture registration, its client-only seed, and a unit assertion. The focused `shot-preview-fixtures` and `shot-plan` suites passed: 158 tests across three files, including the isolated timing file.

I built the UI and started `just serve-noauth` from the task worktree. The first Playwright navigation waited for `networkidle` and timed out because the app maintains an event stream. Switching to `domcontentloaded` and waiting for the actual status toast rendered it successfully. A screenshot showed the message clearly over the Work Queue, and the page reported no JavaScript errors. I inspected the screenshot locally after waiting for the toast’s entry transition to finish.

## Challenges and blockers

The preview server is read-only, so the browser run did not submit a real task. The fixture covers the resulting presentation without creating QA data. Port 7272 was already in use during the first QA pass; I selected an unused port and stopped each helper server after verification.

The round-1 review also reported that its requested `git merge-tree --write-tree` could not create a temporary file. Its own edge-case checklist says the only conflict is `work/1203-qa-pass-new-task-and-update-flows-via-th.md` and explicitly states that close-out resolves this task file from main. I made no manual conflict resolution.

## Key learnings

A screenshot should demonstrate the behavior under review, not only the page where the behavior lives. Client-only shot fixtures provide a safe way to capture transient post-action states when the preview server forbids writes. The fixture must use the same accessible role and message shape as production, and the shot should highlight that exact surface.

Long-lived server connections make `networkidle` an unreliable Playwright readiness signal for this app. Waiting for `domcontentloaded` and then for the expected UI element gives a direct, stable assertion.
